claims.text: A minor Al addition of approximately 0.2–0.5 at.% is an appropriate modification for a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Post-casting heat treatment of the Al-modified alloy will induce an Al-associated precipitate phase.
The induced precipitates will be nanoscale and coherent with the matrix.
Fine precipitates can hinder dislocation motion during high-temperature deformation.
The precipitates can hinder grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature deformation.
Obstruction of dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding by precipitates will produce high-temperature precipitation strengthening.
The Al-modified alloy will have significantly greater high-temperature yield strength than the unmodified alloy at approximately 900°C.
The Al-modified alloy will have a lower creep rate than the unmodified alloy at approximately 900°C.
The strengthening effect should hold under tensile or creep loading at approximately 900°C.
Room-temperature strength and ductility will remain largely unchanged after the Al addition and heat treatment.
Al's low elemental density will limit the density increase caused by the modification.
The Al addition will not adversely affect room-temperature microstructural integrity.
The relevant baseline is an Al-free refractory high-entropy alloy conventionally cast and subjected to the same post-casting heat treatment and testing conditions.
Failure to obtain more than approximately 50% improvement in high-temperature yield strength, or a statistically meaningful creep-rate reduction, would falsify the hypothesis.
A decrease greater than 15% in room-temperature strength or ductility would falsify the hypothesis.
